items.title: Benjamin Watson: 6 Ways to Help Your Kids Define Success

The post Benjamin Watson: 6 Ways to Help Your Kids Define Success appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
Boyd Epley was a pole vaulter who was known for his impressive workout regimen. The University of Nebraska took notice and hired him to be their football strength coach. He quickly had the athletes working harder than ever. He changed their weightlifting routine. He updated team conditioning. And when the Huskers won back-to-back national championships in 1970 and 1971, the rest of the college football world spotted the reason. Rival coaches flew to Lincoln to copy Nebraska’s new methods.

One motivation tool Epley implemented was the giant leaderboards he hung in the weight room. The signs displayed everyone’s weightlifting records. Each player could look up while lifting and see how far they’d come that season. Their progress was trackable. Those signs reminded the players that their individual success, growth, and future were all up to them. That’s a lesson I want my kids to embrace. If comparison is a big thing in your house, or if you want your kids to have a healthy view of achievement, here are 6 ways to help your kids define success.

1. Remember, there will always be someone “better.”

I showed up eager to run at the NFL Combine right after college. I clocked a 4.57 40-yard dash time, which is pretty fast. A few weeks later, at my Georgia Pro Day, I ran even faster—4.41. That time was incredible for me, but it wouldn’t even crack the all-time top 100 pre-draft times recorded.

Our kids need to know they will likely never be the fastest, smartest, tallest, or any other -est. And that’s OK. Are they becoming the best version of themselves? I was never trying to be Usain Bolt. I wasn’t concerned with being the best, just my best. When being No. 1 is the only acceptable outcome, our kids will struggle with their identity. They’ll feel inadequate when they underachieve and start to believe they’ll never be enough. When others’ success becomes the metric by which we measure our own, we’ll often walk away disappointed. Remind your kids to compare themselves to yesterday, not someone else.

2. There’s no cookie-cutter time frame.

Has your child ever worked hard at something like learning to ride a bike or raise their SAT score? What takes one person six hours may take the next person six months. Both timelines can be defined as successful. It all depends on the person. The problem for our kids is that “fastest” is often equated with “best” or “right,” and that’s simply not true.

Learning how to define success for children starts with acknowledging that there is no cookie-cutter version. When helping kids define success, ask them about their desired timeline. Is it relevant to their goal? Can it be done as quickly as they think? Help them see that not everything happens on schedule. Guide them as they do their best, and encourage them for as long as it takes.

3. You get to define success to children.

Do you know how to define success to children? During my time in the NFL, I saw up close how success got defined differently. In 2007, I caught a career-high six touchdowns. My teammate, Randy Moss, also had a career year—23 touchdowns. The final numbers were very different, but we both had successful seasons because we fulfilled different roles on the same team.

Your kids need to learn that same lesson. Success isn’t about matching someone else’s accomplishments; it’s about making the most of their opportunities and abilities. I wasn’t trying to be Randy Moss. He was one of the greatest receivers ever. I was trying to be the best version of myself. That’s how I defined success.

4. Others shouldn’t dictate your happiness.

If your kids’ attitude spikes or dips based on how other people view them or their accomplishments, they’re in for a rough time. Different peer groups will demand different things from your kids. Those subtle influences will tempt your kid to become a chameleon, doing what it takes to fit in. Chasing others’ approval is exhausting.

Kids will feel the pressure to be athletic, smart, funny, and more. When their happiness is tied to peers’ opinions, that’s a recipe for heartache. Kids will begin to question if the successes they do see are “good enough.” If your child spends his or her life trying to satisfy everyone, they’ll be unhappy more often than not. Remind them that being authentic is the goal.

5. Learning to work hard is the reward.

Ask any NFL player, and they’ll tell you that training camp is hard. It’s long days in the sun and a physical beating. I always just wanted the season to start, but I understood that practice produced discipline, resilience, and sacrifice. All of those things are key variables to success. This applies to more than just football. Your kids may not like all the tedious steps that usually precede success, but there are lessons in the grind.

Your kids won’t see the payoff if they don’t embrace the hard work. Better grades don’t just happen. They require studying. Kids must memorize lines if they want a role in the school play. No matter what their goal is, the hard work to get there, even though it’s sometimes unpleasant, isn’t wasted because it’s building toward something great. They won’t feel the satisfaction of achievement without the grind.

6. Failure often precedes success.

Failure and success are intertwined. If your children expect everything to go according to script, remind them that even the most successful people failed in pursuit of their goals.

Will your kids be crushed by failure? Will it deter them? If so, success will be hard to achieve. Successes often follow a pattern of failure and adjustment. The people who get discouraged during the process and fail to persevere are the ones who struggle the most to find success. When your kids fail, remind them they’re not finished. Failure doesn’t have to be their final chapter.

Sound off: Do you know how to define success to children? What would you say?

The post Benjamin Watson: 6 Ways to Help Your Kids Define Success appeared first on All Pro Dad.

items.title: Kurt Warner: 5 Small Moments That Make Great Dads
items.description:
People know me as the Super Bowl MVP and Hall of Fame quarterback. They probably don’t know that I struggled to get on the field in college. I had a good arm and was passionate about games, but the coaches told me the reason I wasn’t seeing much of the field was that I wasn’t [...]

The post Kurt Warner: 5 Small Moments That Make Great Dads appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
People know me as the Super Bowl MVP and Hall of Fame quarterback. They probably don’t know that I struggled to get on the field in college. I had a good arm and was passionate about games, but the coaches told me the reason I wasn’t seeing much of the field was that I wasn’t working hard during practice. At first, it made me angry. Who cared about practice? Then it hit me—most of my time in shoulder pads was spent at practice. I was so focused on the games that I was neglecting the moments that prepared me for them. I’ve never forgotten that lesson.

I’m retired from football now, but not much has changed. Most of fatherhood feels like ordinary reps. Most dads try hard to show up for “big” moments like prom, recitals, and graduations. But 95% of your time as a dad will be “practice” moments. You’ll spend it around the dinner table, driving carpool, or losing in UNO. Your kids know you’ll be there for the big stuff, but they want a dad who is a great practice player too. Here are 5 small moments that make great dads.

1. When You Give Your Kids Attention

When I was in the NFL, my time was a precious resource. I would spend hours at the facility during the day working out and then study game tape at home many nights. Being a pro quarterback demanded a lot from me, but my kids wanted time with me too. So, I’d try to strike a fair balance. When people hear “balance,” they think “even,” but that’s not how I see it. I define balance as giving a kid what they need. I gave them full effort and my undivided attention for as long as I could. That meant no game plans at the dinner table. It meant I’d step away from studying to play with them. My kids knew when it was their time, Dad was all in. I’d put off work because giving them half of me was the same as not being there at all. You don’t have to spend 10 hours per day with your kids to be a good dad, but you do have to give them your full attention when you can. Make time for them and put away distractions.

2. When You Give Your Kids Advice

Three of my kids like football. That was easy for us to talk about. The other four couldn’t care less about football, so giving them advice on their hobbies was a little harder. But I learned that kids don’t need you to be an expert. They need you to be engaged. When you pay attention to what matters to them, you’ll naturally find moments to guide them. I may not know everything about horseback riding or theater or whatever they’re into, but I do know what it means to work hard. I’ve had to handle disappointment. I’ve had to keep showing up when it’s hard. So, if I keep showing up for them, I’ll be perfectly positioned to lend practical advice when they need it. You can do the same. Don’t fall for the trap that only experts have something useful to say.

3. When You Choose to Listen

My kids range from age 20 to 37, so conversations are constantly changing. Some are married. Some are in college. Every conversation looks different. But I try not to do most of the talking. Dads make kids feel heard when they don’t turn every moment into a coaching session. I’ve had to bite my tongue over the years when all they really wanted was for me to sit with them in it, not fix anything. Parenting is hard. Your kids need to know they can bring their hurt, joy, and confusion to you, and you’ll pause and pay attention. Listening before you lecture is how to be a great dad.

4. When You Choose to Learn

I know a ton about throwing a slant and reading defenses. I don’t know much about the equestrian world. At least I didn’t, until one of my twins got interested in riding horses. I watched her interact with these giant animals, and I asked a ton of questions. She got so good that she qualified for the Junior Olympics, which gave me the chance to cheer for her. When you learn about what matters to your kids, they learn that they matter to you. There’s no greater gift than that.

5. When You Tell Them You Love Them

My wife and I knew we weren’t going to be perfect parents, but we were sure going to try. I would constantly ask myself, “Did I do enough?” I wanted to know how to be a great dad, and as I grew, I realized what mattered more than helping with homework was making sure my kids knew, without a doubt, that I loved them. They should never question that. Dads make this happen when we show up consistently, put the kids’ needs above our own, and make sure they feel like Dad is a safe place. We are all going to make mistakes. But if we can remind our kids day after day that we love them more than anything else, we build a bond that outlasts our mistakes.

Sound off: What “practice moments” have you been missing?

In this episode of the All Pro Dad Podcast, the hosts discuss why asking for support from others is essential to becoming a great dad.

items.title: 5 Ways to Treat Your Wife Like She Is Still Your Girlfriend
items.description:
As someone who spends too much time in airports, I have a lot of time to people-watch. When I see a couple who look to be older than 35 being fun, flirtatious, and attentive with each other, I think, I bet they aren’t married. And this is one of the few times I don’t want [...]

The post 5 Ways to Treat Your Wife Like She Is Still Your Girlfriend appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
As someone who spends too much time in airports, I have a lot of time to people-watch. When I see a couple who look to be older than 35 being fun, flirtatious, and attentive with each other, I think, I bet they aren’t married. And this is one of the few times I don’t want to be right. Because if wedding rings are any indicator, I am right about nine times out of 10.

We know this dynamic is not just in airports. We see it in the couple on their phones at dinner. We hear it in the couple fighting two aisles over in Walmart. The great news is we get to choose differently. If you are wondering how to make your wife feel loved and secure, it starts with small, consistent choices. Here are 5 ways to make your wife feel loved and secure, starting today.

1. Listen because you need to know.

My wife, Nancie, has three best friends, and I am convinced they remember every single word the others have ever said. Every. Single. Word. Follow-up questions. Details. The works. Me and my best friends? I’m not a caveman; I remember some things. But every single word? Not a chance.

When you were dating your wife, you listened like you needed the information. Because you did. You wanted to know everything about her. You wanted to know how to love her right. She noticed. It is part of why she said yes. She still wants that guy to show up. Present and tuned in. Not half listening while scrolling. Not waiting for your turn to talk, but actually listening like what she is saying is the most important thing in the room. Because to her, it is. Remember?

2. Date her like you can’t wait to.

Maybe you planned it. Maybe she planned it. But you always did your part and cared about the plan. Because dating was the fun stuff. The good stuff. You got married because you enjoyed each other so much that you decided you wanted to do it for a lifetime. The thing that brought you together is the thing that helps keep you together. She wants to be pursued. Treat her like you would choose her all over again.

The best way to protect your marriage is to enjoy it. So stop waiting for a free night to appear on the calendar. Create one. Because you can’t wait to. Remember?

3. Make her laugh because why wouldn’t you?

At some point, life gets serious. Jobs. Kids. Mortgages. Aging parents. It happens to everyone. And somewhere in the middle of all of it, a lot of us accidentally retire the version of ourselves that made her laugh in the first place.

But here is what we do not want to lose. The guy she fell for. The one who made her laugh. The one who didn’t take himself too seriously. Maybe she married the serious version of you. But she also married the fun one. He’s still in there. Bust him out. I periodically walk out in fluorescent yellow scuba skins when needed. Long story. But it works. It always makes her laugh. Do what makes her laugh.

4. Watch your words because you know they matter.

When you were dating her, you were careful with how you spoke to her. You were trying to win her heart, and you knew what was at stake: your life together. You wanted her to see a man who controlled his temper. Who spoke kindly. Who was gentle with her heart.
She still needs you to be that man. And it is still who you want to be for her. The good news is that you know how. You have already proven it in the biggest of ways. When you watch your words, she feels loved. When she feels loved, she feels secure.

5. Dream together because you found your person.

Maybe dreaming together is part of what brought you together in the first place. You loved talking about the future: what could be. You dreamed about where you would live, what your kids would be like, and what you would name them. You dreamed about the things you would do and the things you wouldn’t.

Nancie and I have four kids, we’ve moved across the country, and we’ve lived in seven different homes. And before any of it became reality, we dreamed it up together. Now, as an almost empty nester, I am learning that the couples who keep dreaming together are the ones who love the season they’re in. We are not done dreaming. Neither are you. And when you keep dreaming together, she feels loved and secure in a way that nothing else quite replaces.

Sound off: What is one thing you do to make sure your wife still feels like your girlfriend?

The post 5 Ways to Treat Your Wife Like She Is Still Your Girlfriend appeared first on All Pro Dad.

items.title: 5 Things That Look Like Strengths but Are Actually Weaknesses
items.description:
I had not heard of the manosphere until a friend mentioned it to me. By then, it was already white hot. When I started digging into the entrenched online movement, it rubbed me the wrong way. The hyper-masculine digital world promotes misogynistic behavior, a status-above-all mindset, and many more harmful things. As the father of [...]

The post 5 Things That Look Like Strengths but Are Actually Weaknesses appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
I had not heard of the manosphere until a friend mentioned it to me. By then, it was already white hot. When I started digging into the entrenched online movement, it rubbed me the wrong way. The hyper-masculine digital world promotes misogynistic behavior, a status-above-all mindset, and many more harmful things. As the father of two girls, I’m trying to teach them what qualities to expect in a man. As a father of a boy, I’m trying to teach him how to be honorable. That’s why the toxic manosphere nonsense infuriates me. If your son is dabbling in the manosphere, it’s time to ask serious questions.

My biggest issue with manosphere content is that it is full of people who want to look strong but are actually weak. Fueled by influencers, boys begin acting and eventually believing the script. Their desire to appear tough and enlightened leads them to put on a strong-man costume. The worst part, our kids see us acting too. We put on a show, behaving a certain way, hoping to trick others. Does this sound familiar? Here are 5 things that look like strengths but are actually weaknesses.

1. Keeping Your Walls Up

I took my family to see an old fort in St. Augustine, Florida. We marveled at its impressive height and the thickness of the stone walls. I remember thinking the fort looked impenetrable because of these huge walls. Walls are meant to keep others out. They’re a great feature for military structures, but a terrible idea for people. You’re not a fortress. When we put up walls, it may look like we can handle anything on our own, but we’re really disguising weakness as strength.

Maybe you put up walls to prevent possible heartache. Maybe they’re meant to prevent people from seeing the real you. That makes sense because high walls do prevent harm, but they also shield us from great things like friendship, growth, and community. In that sense, walls make us weaker. I understand exercising caution when you first meet new people, but if you’re still keeping your walls up at home, work, or in your community year after year, it’s time to think about what you’re trying to protect. An unhealed wound? Your nerves? When your walls are up, it reveals a lack of courage. You have to have strength to show your true self to others. If you keep your walls up, it’ll be difficult for others to really get to know you.

2. Never Showing Emotion

I’ve never been good at showing my emotions. It’s not that I have none; I just tend to muscle through sad moments and pretend stress isn’t real. My wife calls me out on it because she knows me well. I don’t think my kids are aware that I actually do feel things. That’s not me bragging. That’s admitting I’m weak in this area.

It’s good to let people know how you’re feeling. Hiding in the garage when you’re stressed or acting unfazed when you get bad news isn’t good for you. You need to let those feelings out. Men tend to express anger often because it’s socially acceptable. But every other feeling is valid, and you shouldn’t be tricked into thinking suppression is strength. When you show your emotions, you give your kids (and others) permission to be real around you, not walk on eggshells to avoid expressing themselves in ways Dad never does. That will help them handle their emotions better. Lead by example in this area.

3. Not Saying “I’m Sorry”

As BJ Foster pointed out on the All Pro Dad podcast, “Strong people apologize quickly.” That’s because they have the real strength of humility. That’s the subtle superpower we should be aiming for. Apologies begin to fix what’s broken between you and someone else. Withholding that apology, or failing to ever say “I’m sorry,” is weakness masquerading as righteousness. It stings to admit you’re wrong. It’s not fun. But strong people do it quickly.

Our kids need to hear us apologize, see us do it with others, and understand that humility is strength. Refusing to apologize and “sticking to your guns” when you know you’re wrong is just disguising weakness as strength.

4. Doing Everything Yourself

I remember getting lost on a road trip with some buddies while in college. We were trying to get from North Carolina to Florida, and our MapQuest printouts were insufficient. So, there we stood on the side of the highway in Athens, with the glovebox map sprawled out on the hood, silently wondering if any of us had the guts to go into the gas station and ask for directions. Doing so would mean we’d have to rely on others for help, and that certainly wasn’t going to happen. Eventually, we made it home.

I don’t struggle with this anymore because smartphones have GPS. But I still don’t ask for help much. That’s not a sign of strength. Relying on others has benefits, such as sharing burdens, receiving encouragement, and understanding that you aren’t made for isolation. Avoiding asking for help is a recipe for loneliness and frustration. That’s why Solomon, a king in the Bible who many consider the wisest man ever, wrote, “Two are better than one because they have a good return for their labor. If either of them falls down, one can help the other up. But pity anyone who falls and has no one to help them up.” It’s time to reject the idea that strong men don’t ask for help.

5. Never Being Vulnerable

I have a scar on my forehead. I’d have to pull my hair back for you to see it, but it’s there. You’d never know I had a horrible bike accident when I was five, and the wound required 17 stitches—unless I told you. That scar is part of my story, but only I decide if it’s told. There’s a big difference between a physical mark and an emotional, mental, or spiritual one, but we all have them. Sometimes men fall into the trap of thinking that if we choose not to expose our flaws or mistakes, they’ll just magically disappear. But that’s not true. It takes true strength to show people who you really are.

Being vulnerable isn’t weakness. It’s the only way you’ll ever become fully known. That may sound scary, but vulnerability cracks the door open for friendship, something men struggle with. Your kids will struggle, too, if they keep things hidden from others. Encourage them to be honest with others and share what’s true about themselves.

Sound off: Where are you disguising weakness as strength?

The post 5 Things That Look Like Strengths but Are Actually Weaknesses appeared first on All Pro Dad.

items.title: 7 Things We Get Wrong About Parenting Teens
items.description:
I recently typed “parenting teens is…” in the search bar on Safari. The results auto-populated as follows: “hard,” “exhausting,” “so hard.” Parenting teens isn’t for the faint of heart. Whether it’s the natural desire for teens to differentiate themselves from you, the changing cultural trends that you struggle to understand, let alone keep up with, [...]

The post 7 Things We Get Wrong About Parenting Teens appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
I recently typed “parenting teens is…” in the search bar on Safari. The results auto-populated as follows: “hard,” “exhausting,” “so hard.” Parenting teens isn’t for the faint of heart. Whether it’s the natural desire for teens to differentiate themselves from you, the changing cultural trends that you struggle to understand, let alone keep up with, or the overall pace of life teens keep today, it is not easy to be a parent of teens.

But the objectively difficult work of parenting teens is made even harder because of the false stories we tell ourselves. There are lies we tend to believe that leave us thinking the best we can do is survive the teenage years and hope our kids do too. But what if those stories are wrong? Here are 7 things we get wrong about parenting teens.

1. There’s one right way to do it.

Look, I think you should read books and articles about parenting teens (thank you for reading this one), but what you shouldn’t do is assume that some author somewhere has a formula for you so that you can raise teens who turn out to be model citizens and think you’re their hero. There’s no “one way” to parent. You are unique. So is your teen. The combination of two unique people will undoubtedly give birth to a unique parent-child relationship. This is beautiful and good, but also hard. So learn all you can from as many sources as you can, but in the end, love your teen deeply and give yourself lots of grace. You’ll need it.

2. Your teen’s choices are a reflection of your parenting.

Certainly, having good parents matters a lot. But it doesn’t guarantee anything. I’ve sat with remarkable parents who were brokenhearted over teens who ran away from home, battled addiction, or even took their own lives. Yet, they had other teenagers in their family who were “model” youth who loved their parents deeply and couldn’t understand why their siblings responded the way they did. Your job is to love your teens and do all you can to point them in the right direction. You can’t, and shouldn’t, control them. This is why parenting teens is not for the faint of heart. Your teen’s choices are not a reflection of your parenting.

3. It shouldn’t be this hard.

Think of something worth doing. Maybe it’s running a marathon, losing weight, or getting your Ph.D. What do all of those things have in common? They are hard. If they weren’t, everyone would do them. Almost everything worth doing is hard. Giving birth is the perfect metaphor for this. One of the most difficult things a person can do is also necessary for life itself. Of course, stewarding the life of another person as that person learns what it means to be himself is hard. But you’re up for the challenge.

4. Teens are mindless adapters.

I think it’s easy to believe teens are simply mindless adapters, uncritically engaging with whatever the culture says is “cool” in the moment. However, many teens are showing a willingness to make what seem like radically countercultural choices. For example, observers of culture have noted a growing number of teens and young adults opting for “dumb phones” and digital cameras to step away from the ever-present smartphone. Additionally, despite its prevalence in our culture, both drinking and sexual activity appear to be at historic lows for teens. While it’s certainly a complex picture, there is hope that parenting teens toward countercultural choices may not be a lost cause.

5. Teens are resilient.

This phrase gets thrown around a lot. But the fact is that teens aren’t automatically resilient. However, every teen has the capacity to build resilience. The difference here is one of intention. You can’t rest on the idea that your teen can handle the bullying or the breakup or the stress she’s experiencing just because she’s young and intelligent. She needs you to walk with her, listen well, and encourage her so that she can become the kind of person who is resilient.

6. Agreeable teens are best.

Agreeable teens are definitely the easiest. But that may not be what you want in the long run. It turns out that, according to research, kids who are willing to argue with their parents are also more willing to argue with their peers when they try to influence them. So what makes life easier at home may not be what’s best “out in the world.” If parenting teens feels like one battle after another right now, take heart. These battles are preparing him for the real fight he has outside your home.

7. Teens hate their parents.

Between arguing with you constantly, hiding out in their room, and the eye rolls, it’s easy to think your teen can’t stand you. While of course there are times when both of you might need a break from one another, a recent survey showed that 89% of teens actually think highly of their dads and over 75% enjoy spending time with them. So don’t lose heart when your teen seems like he hates you. It’s more than likely just the opposite.

Sound off: What other narratives about parenting teens have you found to be false?

The post 7 Things We Get Wrong About Parenting Teens appeared first on All Pro Dad.
